title: MA7-09671
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant is XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. She is a 28-year-old citizen of Mexico who is claiming refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and 97 (1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

In her original Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative, the claimant based her claim on that of her brother, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, who feared a man called XXXXX. XXXXX had been carrying out an opinion poll for an upcoming election, when he was asked by XXXXX to give him information how the results were going. When he refused, he began to receive threats at home. On XXXXXXX, 2007, XXXXX went to the police to report the threats and then bought a ticket and left for Canada on XXXXXXX, 2007.

After XXXXX left for Canada, the claimant's other brother, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, began receiving threats to return the information that his brother XXXXX had collected regarding the elections. Because of these threats XXXX left for Canada on XXXXXXX, 2007.

Once her brothers had left Mexico, the claimant began receiving threats from XXXXXX. On XXXXXXX, 2007, XXXXXX called her at home. She told him her brothers were out of the country. On XXXXXXX, 2007, he called her at work and threatened her once again. The claimant told her parents who suggested that she leave for Mexico City for some time. The claimant left that same evening. On XXXXXXX, 2007, her father called her to say that two men had come to the place where she worked to inquire about her and he suggested that she leave Mexico and to join her brothers in Canada. The claimant arrived in Canada on XXXXXXX, 2007 and claimed refugee protection. These were the allegations according to the claimant's original PIF narrative, signed by the claimant on February 1, 2008.

It was disclosed in the file that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX had withdrawn his claim for refugee protection on March 24, 2009. The hearing for refugee protection for XXXXXX and the claimant was originally scheduled for November 5, 2010. The comments of the RPD member in the file state that the claimant broke down in tears at the beginning of the hearing and stated that she had been a victim of rape. The hearing was postponed because of the psychological state of the claimant.
XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX then withdrew his claim for refugee protection on December 10, 2010.

A new hearing for the claimant was scheduled for June 8, 2011 but counsel requested a postponement because of the comments of the psychologist on May 31, 2011 that the claimant was in distress and that during the interview with the psychologist on that day she had disclosed details of sexual abuse that she had not disclosed in the past and which were related to her fear of returning to Mexico. The psychologist recommended a 10-12 week delay to allow for the claimant to receive crisis intervention in psychotherapy and medication for her anxiety. Counsel's request for postponement was accepted by the coordinating member. The coordinating member noted that the hearing of November 5, 2010 was postponed because of the psychological state of the claimant, but that surprisingly medication was not begun until the end of May 2011. The next hearing was set on a peremptory basis and scheduled for September 12, 2011.
On May 19, 2011 counsel submitted a modification to the claimant's PIF narrative. ALLEGATIONS (according to the modified PIF narrative, dated May 19, 2011)

The claimant alleges that she became acquainted with XXXXXXXXXXXXX and her common-law husband, XXXXXXXX, in XXXXX 2006 in the city of XXXXXXXX. She was intrigued by the fact that the couple would ask her for money from time to time to buy food for their children and yet at the same time, they were able to drive luxurious vehicles. She also found it odd that Mrs. XXXXXXX had once told her that she had beaten women who displayed an interest in her husband. Despite these warning signals, the claimant nevertheless continued her friendship with the couple.

In mid- XXXXXXX 2006, the claimant received a call from XXXXXX to come to the XXX XXXX police headquarters with 1,500 pesos, in order to pay bail for his wife who had been detained. The money was returned to her by XXXXXXXXXX on the same day as the police commander had allowed Ms. XXXXXXX to go free without paying bail.

The claimant began to distance herself from the couple on the advice of her parents. On XXXXXX, 2007, the claimant accepted an invitation to the couple's home. A friend of XXXXXXX XXXX was also there and his name was "XXXXX". The claimant drank tequila that was offered to her and began to feel dizzy. She was beaten and kicked by XXXXXXXXX and "XXXXX". The two men then proceeded to rape her several times.

Following the rape, the two men took her home in their car. The claimant needed medical attention. She wanted to report the rape to the police but hesitated because she was afraid of revenge from the perpetrators who had physically and sexually abused her.

The claimant stopped attending university in XXXXXX 2007. She started receiving strange phone calls, which she thought may have been from the two men who raped her. The claimant's father took the decision to send her to stay with her aunt in Mexico City. Frightened by the threats that Mr. XXXX and "XXXXX" had made to her, she decided to leave Mexico and come to Canada on XXXXXXX, 2007.
On the basis of the evidence presented, the panel finds that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" nor is she a "person in need of protection".
The identity and citizenship of the claimant were established to the satisfaction of the panel on the basis of her Mexican passport on record.

On September 6, 2011, the RPD received a request to have the claimant designated a vulnerable person. On September 8, 2011, because of the claimant's psychological state, she was identified as such in accordance with Directive # 8 and the procedural changes outlined in paragraph 4.2 of this directive were followed.1 Counsel began with the questioning of the claimant and the member asked questions when it was felt that additional clarification was required. The panel ensured that the hearing was conducted in a calm and reassuring atmosphere and exercised care, so that the questions would not be perceived as intimidating or adversarial. Despite her having been declared a vulnerable person, the panel found that the claimant testified in a clear and coherent manner. She was calm and composed and showed no difficulty with concentration. While she may have shed a few tears at one moment, she was well in control of her emotions, did not break down at all at the hearing, and was also able to remember dates and describe events.

Before making its findings of fact and assessing the credibility of the claimant's allegations, the panel carefully reviewed the IRB Chairperson's Guideline on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution2. The panel is aware that, when making findings concerning the credibility of a woman who alleges that she has been a victim of gender violence, it must display knowledge, understanding and sensitivity with respect to the reality of women who find themselves in such situations.

The panel also considered the detailed psychological report, presented as Exhibit D-1, which states that the debasing treatment at the hands of her former friends has left the claimant with feelings of shame and inadequacy. The psychologist states that it was this profound shame which prevented the claimant from revealing that she was a victim of a brutal sexual assault and that she did not confide in anybody because of this deep sense of shame and guilt.

The panel finds that the determinative issues in this case were credibility and whether there is an objective basis to the claimant's fear of persecution. The possibility of an internal flight alternative was also examined.

At the beginning of the hearing the claimant stated that she feared the trio, XXXXXXXXXX, her husband, XXXXXXX, and their friend "XXXXX" who had brutally attacked and raped her on the night of XXXXXX, 2007. Considering that her first PIF narrative had been based on a fear of XXX XXX, the claimant was asked if she also feared this man. The claimant stated that she has a fear of him as well because she fears that XXXXX might be linked with the trio in some way. The claimant stated however that she did not have any proof of the link between XXXXX and the trio. When asked then why she would think that there would be a connection of some sort between them, the claimant replied that it was because the phone calls from XXXXX had begun one month after she had been raped. It was pointed out to the claimant by the panel that in her original PIF narrative she had stated that the calls from XXXXX had begun only after her brothers had left the country which was some eight months later. The claimant then stated that the first call she received from XXXXX was on XXXXXX, 2007, which coincides with what had been indicated in her original PIF. Counsel for the claimant provided a great deal of information, presented as Exhibit D-6, on the problems that victims of torture may have in trying to recollect the sequence of events and argued at the end of the hearing in his submissions that the fact that the claimant had placed XXXXX's call one month after the rape, should not have a negative inference on her credibility, considering the horrific events that she had experienced. The panel does not agree.

The claimant was able to state with precision that the first call from XXXXX was received on XXXXXX, 2007. The panel found that her earlier statement that the call from XXXXX had occurred one month after the rape was an attempt on the part of the claimant to answer the question why she would assume that there was a link between XXXXX and the trio who had attacked her. When asked if the claimant believed that XXXX and her husband were involved in any kind of organized crime, the claimant replied that while she did not have any proof, she suspected that they were dealing in stolen cars. XXXXX had allegedly been interested in the claimant's brother XXXXX because of her brother's knowledge of the election opinion survey results. The claimant testified that she did not know XXXXX and had never seen him, he was never in the company of the trio, and there was no evidence presented which would indicate that there was any link between them. The panel did not find the claimant credible when she appeared to suggest that XXXXX and the trio were linked in some way. The panel believes rather that her suggestion of a link on the basis of XXXXX's phone call received a month after the rape was an attempt on the part of the claimant to cover the fact that the first PIF narrative contained a completely different story than the modified version.

The claimant testified that her brothers, XXXXX and XXXX, have both since returned to Mexico after withdrawing their refugee claims. She testified that XXXX had returned because he felt that enough time had elapsed and that he would no longer be in danger.

The claimant stated that XXXXX did not speak to her after the claimant had pronounced in the hearing room on XXXXXX, 2010 that she had been raped. XXXXX withdrew his refugee claim the following month.

The claimant was asked why she had not mentioned the rape when she claimed refugee protection. She replied that she was feeling shame and that she could speak of it to no one. The claimant's PIF describes that the claimant was badly beaten on the night of the alleged rape and that her eyes were swollen and that she had bruises all over her body. At the hearing, the claimant pointed to two scars she had on her left arm, which she says were also the result of her injuries on that day. The claimant lived with her parents and brothers and stated that they were aware of the fact that she had been badly beaten. The claimant had stayed in bed for 15 days to recover. The claimant stated that because of her shame she had not told her parents or her brothers of the rape.

Considering that she was too ashamed to speak of the rape, the claimant was then asked why she would not at least have mentioned to the immigration officer that she had been brutally beaten and attacked by XXXXXXXXXXX and "XXXXX". The claimant was not able to answer this question to the satisfaction of the panel. She stated she did not know why she did not state this at the time she made her claim. The claimant went on to say that she was not aware of the refugee process and that she had told the immigration officials what her brothers had told her to say, which was the story about XXXXX and his threats.

While the panel understands that women who have been raped may feel shame to reveal what has happened to them, the panel finds that the claimant, had she feared harm from the trio of XXXXX XXXXXXX, XXXXXXX and "XXXXX", would have been able at least to tell the officer about the physical beatings. The trio had threatened her that they would harm her and her family members if she spoke to anyone about what had happened. The claimant's parents and brothers all lived together and they were already aware that it was XXXX who had inflicted the injuries on the claimant and the physical beating was therefore not something that she needed to hide from her brothers. The panel finds that if the claimant feared the trio and that if this was the reason for her departure from Mexico, it would have been expected that she would have been able to mention at least some aspects of this fear at the time of her refugee claim.

In the claimant's immigration interview on December 30, 2007, there were variations in the story as presented to the immigration officer and with what her brother XXXXX had presented in his PIF narrative which was included as Exhibit A-2. The claimant stated at the interview that she was threatened by XXXXX on XXXXX, 2007 and that she received a threat at work from him on XXXXX, 2007. In her first PIF narrative these dates had been changed for XXXXX, 2007 and XXXXX, 2007, presumably to correspond with XXXXX's PIF narrative, which showed that the brother had received threats which caused him to leave Mexico on XXXXXX. XXXX then became the object of threats by XXXXX. After his departure for Canada, it was the claimant who then allegedly began receiving threats from XXXXX. The panel finds this discrepancy in the dates given by the claimant in her interview and in her original PIF, attests to the lack of credibility of the claimant's story about XXXXX.

The panel finds that the claimant knew that XXXX, who had based his claim on the same story, had withdrawn his refugee claim. XXXXX withdrew his refugee claim one month after the November 5, 2007 hearing when the claimant announced her rape. Had XXXXX feared harm at the hands of XXXXX, it is doubtful that he would have withdrawn his claim and returned to Mexico.

While the claimant may have feared revealing the rape to her brothers, the panel does not find it credible that, in the context of her refugee claim, a story involving a serious beating causing severe bodily injury to the claimant would have been ignored in favour of a story where the claimant had to leave the country because of two telephone calls from XXXXX. The panel does not accept the claimant's explanation that she did not know the refugee process. The claimant is an educated woman who made a separate refugee claim from her brothers and had the opportunity to explain the true reasons for her fears. Had she experienced severe physical injuries, as she alleges, it is surprising to the panel that she would not have mentioned this when asked about her fears of returning to Mexico. While the claimant stated that she did not know when XXXXX had come to the decision to withdraw his claim, the panel finds that the story of the alleged rape and beating in XXXXX 2007 was, on a balance of probabilities, an attempt to bolster her claim for refugee protection, considering that one of her brothers had already withdrawn his claim based on the same story and returned to Mexico and that the other brother was about to do the same.

The panel considered the psychological report, Exhibit D-1, which describes the psychological distress of the claimant. The psychological report on page 4 mentions that for many months after her arrival to Canada the claimant "suffered from nervous crisis during which she was unable to stop crying to the point that her respiratory system closes down. At those times she becomes unable to breathe and feels that she is suffocating. Anxiety mounts and she feels like screaming. At one point she needed medical care in a local hospital". Counsel also presented exhibit D-2 which is a medical report, dated XXXXX, 2008, when the claimant was taken by ambulance to the emergency department of a Montreal hospital in just such a state of anxiety. This report mentions that the claimant's condition occurred as a result of a "chicane de famille" or family argument. The panel finds that many stressful situations can cause anxiety and the reactions described. When asked about what factor was the trigger on that particular day, the claimant testified that she was a witness to an argument between her two brothers XXXX and XXXXX. She then stated that every time she is a witness to friction of any kind it triggers in her mind memories of the time she was raped. The panel finds that an argument between two brothers when the claimant is alone in the country with only these two family members would be an anxiety provoking incident and accepts the diagnosis of anxiety but does not accept that it is tied to the allegations of the claimant.

The claimant alleges that she was brutally beaten and raped. She stated that she did not go to a physician in Mexico apart from an ophthalmologist whom she saw the day after the rape. This report from the ophthalmologist was presented as Exhibit D-4. The claimant testified that while she did not tell the doctor about the rape, she did tell him that she had been attacked by XXXX and that he had told her that she should go to the authorities to file a complaint. Surprisingly the report does not mention that the claimant was a victim of a physical attack by another individual but mentions only that she received several blows to her temporal frontal region caused by a solid object. While the claimant may have indeed suffered some injury in XXXXX 2007 and needed to consult an ophthalmologist, the panel does not find that this medical report corroborates her story that the injury inflicted on her was the result of an attack by the trio.

The claimant reported that she was traumatized after the rape in XXXXX 2007 and that as a result she missed classes and did not get her diploma. Yet in her IMM 5474 form completed shortly after her arrival to Canada, in response to question 6, the claimant had stated that she finished her studies in XXXXX 2007 and that she had obtained a diploma in XXXXX. The claimant was asked to examine the form and she declared that it was filled out in her own handwriting. When asked why she had put down that she had obtained a degree she said it had been a mistake. The panel does not accept that the claimant would have made this mistake. While at the hearing, the claimant stated she had missed classes and was unable to study because of what had happened to her, the panel noted that the claimant continued to work at her full time job until XXXXX 2007, despite the trauma she had allegedly suffered. Exhibit D-5 is a letter from her employer attesting to the fact that the claimant continued to work until XXXXX 2007.

Even if the panel had found the claimant's allegations to be credible, since refugee protection is forward looking the panel also finds that the claimant would not have a well-founded fear of persecution today. The claimant was asked when the last time was that she had seen XXXX, her husband and "XXXX". She replied that she had seen them only twice since XXXXX 2007 and that on both occasions it was at a distance. They did not approach her and she has not spoken to them since the attack on XXXXX, 2007. She also testified that they had never come to her house to look for her. The claimant was asked if they had ever come to her father's store but she stated that her father had closed his store. When asked why, she stated it was for economic reasons, so it would not appear that the reason for his store closure was related to the problems with XXXX. The claimant stated that XXXX and her husband had tried to call her by phone but that she would always hang up. She herself stated that while she had about 10 calls in all from them in the days following the incident in XXXXX 2007, these calls occurred with decreasing frequency as time went on. No threats were issued. The claimant stated that when she heard a voice on the other line she would simply hang up. She reported also that they had called her once on the phone at work but that she also had hung up at that time.

The claimant also testified that after her beating in XXXXX 2007, neighbours had come to her father's store and told him that they had often seen women go into XXXX's home and that they could also hear the sounds of women screaming from time to time. The claimant was asked if she suspected that this type of behaviour was a pattern with the trio and the claimant replied that she had suspicions that they had been doing bad things but that she had not imagined the extent of their crimes.

The claimant was asked why the trio would want to harm her today. The claimant stated that she believes that they are angry with her because she was friends with them and then suddenly withdrew from them and that they then felt rejected as a result. The claimant stated that they wanted reprisals. Yet the claimant did not make a complaint on the trio to the police, which would have caused problems for the trio if an investigation had been launched. Since no police report was made, an important element of the reprisal theory is missing. The panel rejects the feeling that the trio felt rejected, because had this been a pattern of behaviour on the part of XXXX that they would lure victims by first befriending them and later harming them, according to her testimony it would appear that the trio has gone on to other victims. Since their actions would appear to be based on first establishing a friendship with the victim, the claimant's decision not to have any further contact with them would thereby make it difficult for them to continue to operate in their usual way.

The claimant described that XXXX had connections with the chief of police in XXXXXXXX and gave this as a reason why she did not report the rape to the authorities. She described the incident in XXXXXX 2006 when she was called by XXXXXXXX to bring 1,500 pesos as bail money for XXXX's release from jail. The claimant said she gave this money to XXXX in her jail cell. The claimant was asked why she had not given the money to the police officer when she arrived at the jail house, considering that she had been called to the jail in order to ensure XXXX's release. The claimant responded that she had simply asked for XXXX and that she had been directed to her cell. The claimant believes that XXXX is connected with the chief of police since she was released from jail three hours later and was able to give the claimant back the money saying that the chief of police had helped her. The panel found this story odd and asked the claimant why she would have been asked by XXXX's husband to get the money in the first place when the police commander could have been contacted directly. The claimant stated that XXXX would not have been sure if the police commander was on duty that night. The panel believes that had XXXX the police connections she claimed to have, her partner, XXXXXXXX, would have also been in a position to contact the police commander that night to secure her release. The panel did not find the story credible and finds that the XXXXXX 2006 incident may have been an attempt on the claimant to bolster her story to make it appear that she was dealing with criminals who had connections to the police.

After the alleged event in XXXXXX 2007, the claimant remained in her home until XXXXX 2007 and was not harmed by the trio again. The trio did not even come looking for her at her home. It is now 2011 and four years have passed. The panel does not find that, on a balance of probabilities, that the trio would have any interest in pursuing the claimant today. If the trio operates on a plan of befriending young women only to harm them later, the claimant's lack of desire to have contact with the trio would make it difficult for them to continue their pattern of behaviour. The panel finds that had the trio been intent on harming her again, they would have had the opportunity to do so in the months following the XXXXX 2007 incident until her departure from XXXXXXXX some eight months later.

The panel took into consideration the psychological report but did not find the claimant credible that she had been raped and beaten by the trio. Rather the panel found that it was an attempt to save her refugee claim considering that one of her brother's had already withdrawn his claim and returned to Mexico. Even if the panel had believed the story of the rape by the trio, it would not appear that the trio would have the motivation and desire to continue to harm her some four years later, especially considering that there were new victims for them to prey on.

Even if the panel had believed the claimant's allegations of rape and brutality by the trio, the panel finds that nevertheless an internal flight alternative would have been available to the claimant in Mexico City. The claimant had gone to Mexico City for a month before her departure to Canada and she was not harmed there.

The test to be applied in determining whether there is an IFA is two-pronged: (i) there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the proposed IFA area and (ii) conditions in the IFA area must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, for the claimant to seek refuge there.3

The panel found that the claimant would not be of interest to the trio today and that therefore they would have little interest in conducting a search to find her. The panel did not find the incident with the bail money to be credible. No other credible evidence was presented that XXXX had connections in the police force who would be able to help the trio in their search for the claimant. |Furthermore, the claimant herself had testified that an aunt in XXXXXXXXX had told XXXX that the claimant is now in Canada. Knowing this XXXX and her husband would have even less reason to begin to search for the claimant in Mexico, a country with 112 million inhabitants. Should the claimant fear returning to XXXXXXXXX, the panel finds that she would have an internal flight alternative in Mexico City. She is an educated young woman with a university education and training in XXXXXXX. The panel finds it would be possible for her to live in Mexico City. The claimant also has an aunt in the city and she had stayed with her for a month prior to her departure to Canada where no harm had come to her. The panel considered the claimant's vulnerability and finds that the claimant would not be alone in the city. Furthermore Mexico City had a number of good psychologists to help the claimant to deal with her issues involving anxiety. The panel determines that it is not unreasonable for the claimant to move to Mexico City as the conditions in the proposed IFA would not jeopardize the life or safety of the claimant.

Because of the issue with credibility, the fact that the claimant does not have a well-founded fear of harm today and because of the possibility of an IFA in Mexico City, the panel finds that there is not a serious possibility that the claimant would be persecuted should she return to Mexico today and finds that she is not a "Convention refugee" according to section 96 of the IRPA. For the same reasons, on a balance of probabilities, the panel finds that the claimant would not be subjected to a danger of torture or to a risk to life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, should she return to Mexico and that she is not a "person in need of protection" according to section 97 (1) of the same Act.

The panel determines that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX is neither a "Convention refugee" nor is she a "person in need of protection". The panel, therefore, rejects her claim.
